metadata.title: TIMSS 2014/15 Mathematics Year 5: Trends over 20 years in TIMSS (New Zealand report)
metadata.venue: educationcounts.govt.nz (New Zealand Ministry of Education / Comparative Education Research Unit)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report uses TIMSS 2014/15 middle primary (Year 5) mathematics data for New Zealand and compares results to other participating countries. Because TIMSS uses a multistage sampling design (schools sampled within explicit strata; classes sampled with equal probability within schools; all Year 5 students within sampled classes), the report applies TIMSS sampling weights to produce estimates representative of the Year 5 student population. The overall sampling weight is described as a product of school, class, and student weights, and the report notes that means are weighted accordingly. The manuscript does not provide a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that weighting is required due to sampling.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report describes TIMSS scaling and the use of item response theory to infer achievement on a common scale, but it does not document a specific missing-data strategy for student responses (e.g., complete-case deletion vs imputation). Because the document is a national benchmarking/reporting document rather than an ML study, it does not provide the level of methodological detail needed to classify missing-data handling. This is therefore treated as a reporting gap for missing-data procedures.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report analyzes TIMSS 2014/15 middle primary mathematics for New Zealand Year 5 students assessed in October–November 2014. Schools were sampled separately for Year 5 and Year 9 with the intent to minimize overlap; for Year 5, schools were sampled from explicit strata based on decile and level of urbanisation. Within each sampled school, classes were sampled with equal probability and all Year 5 students within each sampled class were selected. New Zealand exclusions were applied at both school and within-school levels: school-level exclusions included very small schools (<4 Year 5 students), special education schools, the Correspondence School, and schools providing >50% of instruction in te reo Māori; within-school exclusions included special education classes, special needs students, students with insufficient instruction in English, and units providing >50% of instruction in te reo Māori. The report also notes an international guideline that countries should keep excluded students to a maximum of 5% of the target population, and it reports a New Zealand exclusion rate of 4.8% for Year 5.

data.outcome_summary: This New Zealand technical benchmarking report summarizes TIMSS 2014/15 mathematics results for Year 5 (middle primary) students, administered as a pencil-and-paper test in two timed sessions (36 minutes each) with both multiple-choice and constructed-response items. Achievement is placed on the TIMSS scale (mean 500, SD 100) using item response theory and is interpreted using international benchmarks at 400 (low), 475 (intermediate), 550 (high), and 625 (advanced). The report compares New Zealand’s mean achievement across cycles (1994/95 to 2014/15) and against other participating countries, and it also reports equity patterns using benchmark classifications (e.g., 6% advanced; 16% below low). It further discusses curriculum relevance via test–curriculum matching and reports that when the test was reduced to items appropriate to New Zealand Year 5 curriculum expectations, the average student answered less than half correctly. Methodologically, the report emphasizes that TIMSS sampling weights (school/class/student) are applied and that standard errors reflect both sampling uncertainty and uncertainty from inferring proficiency from a subset of items; however, it does not provide missing-data handling details.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a national reporting/benchmarking report rather than an empirical machine-learning study. It does not train or evaluate predictive ML models, and it does not specify a target-variable prediction pipeline; therefore, fields related to ML techniques and structured predictive findings are intentionally empty. The report also provides extensive assessment and sampling methodology (including weighting and scaling) but does not document missing-data handling procedures at the level required for PV/missing-data classification in an ML context.
